lead: The method of superposition solves a beam with several loads by splitting them into simple cases, finding the deflection or slope for each case from a standard result, and adding the answers algebraically. It exists because a linear elastic beam responds in proportion to load, so the effect of a combined load is the sum of the effects of its parts. Engineers use it for quick checks on floor beams, overhanging shafts and bridge girders.
prereq: You need the elastic curve (Chapter 5.1) and the moment-area method (Chapter 5.4); double integration (Chapter 5.2) gives the standard results.

blocks.text: For a linear elastic beam, bending moment is linear in the applied loads. Curvature is M/EI, and two integrations give slope and deflection, so both are linear in the loads. If load case 1 gives deflection δ<sub>1</sub> at a point and load case 2 gives δ<sub>2</sub> at the same point, the combined case gives δ<sub>1</sub> + δ<sub>2</sub> there. This is the superposition principle. It needs small deflections, a linear elastic material and unchanged geometry. Only a few universities teach it as a separate topic.

head: Beam and load
Maximum deflection
rows: Simply supported, central point load P

blocks.text: Here L is span in m, P is point load in kN, w is UDL in kN/m, and EI is flexural rigidity in kN·m². Each result is downward for downward loads.

Write the combined loading as a sum of standard cases. Find the deflection at the required point for each case. Take downward deflections as positive and upward deflections as negative, then add algebraically. The same rule works for slopes, positive meaning rotation of the free end downwards.

items: Sketch each standard case alone; keep the same span and EI.
Compute δ for each case at the same point.
Take downward as positive and upward as negative; add algebraically.

For an overhanging beam, keep the whole beam (span plus overhang) as one structure and split only the loading into standard cases. The deflection of the overhang free end equals the overhang length times the slope at the support (from the main-span cases) plus the bending deflection of the overhang under its own load.

blocks.text: Never add a midspan deflection from one case to a quarter-span deflection from another. The point must be the same. Superposition still holds for a stepped or tapered beam, but each standard result assumes constant EI over the span it is applied to. Divide such a beam into constant-EI segments, or use an energy method. Superposition genuinely fails only for nonlinear material, for large deflections that change the geometry, or for a change of structural system, such as a support lifting off.

figure.caption: The two standard cases act at the same midspan point; their deflections add to 20.25 mm downward.

examples.question: A simply supported beam of span 6 m carries a UDL of 4 kN/m over the whole span and a central point load of 12 kN. EI = 6000 kN·m². Find the midspan deflection by superposition.
steps: Check linear elastic, small-deflection conditions; superposition is valid.
Case 1, central point load: δ<sub>1</sub> = PL³/(48EI) = (12 × 6³)/(48 × 6000) = 2592/288000 = 0.009 m = 9 mm downward.
Both act at midspan and in the same direction. Take downward as positive: δ = (+9) + (+11.25) = +20.25 mm, the plus sign meaning downward.
examples.answer: The midspan deflection is 20.25 mm downward.

traps: Adding deflections at different points; superposition works at one point at a time.
Dropping the sign when a load acts upward or opposite to another; add algebraically.
Using the cantilever formula for a simply supported beam, or forgetting the 5 in 5wL⁴/384EI.
Mixing units: L in mm with EI in kN·m² gives a wrong deflection; convert to metres first.
Applying superposition to a nonlinear or large-deflection problem where geometry changes.

quiz.q: State the superposition principle for beam deflections.
quiz.a: At a point, the deflection from combined loads equals the algebraic sum of deflections from each load acting alone, for a linear elastic beam.

quiz.q: Write the midspan deflection of a simply supported beam under full UDL w.
Why does superposition require linear elasticity?
quiz.a: Deflection is proportional to load only when M/EI and the integrations stay linear; yielding or nonlinear material breaks proportionality.

quiz.q: Cantilever, L = 2 m, end load 5 kN, EI = 2000 kN·m². Find end deflection.
Simply supported span 4 m, UDL 6 kN/m, EI = 4000 kN·m². Find midspan deflection.
A simply supported beam has a downward UDL and an upward central point load. How do you find midspan deflection?
quiz.a: Compute downward UDL deflection and upward point-load deflection at midspan, assign opposite signs, add algebraically, and check which dominates.

quiz.q: Give two situations where superposition is unsafe.
quiz.a: (i) Large deflections that change the load arms or the geometry. (ii) Material yielding or other non-Hookean behaviour, so deflection is no longer proportional to load. A third: a change of structural system, such as a support that lifts off or a contact that opens.

beyond: Not for the exam. Superposition leads to influence lines, where the ordinate at a section gives the effect of a unit load at any position. It also supports moving-load analysis for bridges and crane girders. Search for 'influence line ordinates' and 'Müller-Breslau principle' next.
